household: with Miss Peters and Miss Nettie
creator: Ruth Sawyer
address_as_given: the Misses Peters' apartment, two flights up, on Thirty-Ninth Street
notes: Ten-year-old Lucinda boards for a year with Miss Peters and Miss Nettie while her parents are in Italy; the diary entries are dated only '189-'. The novel gives Thirty-Ninth Street but no number or avenue; the point sits between Sixth and Seventh Avenues because Lucinda skates to Bryant Park, to Eighth Avenue, and to the Gedney House hotel 'two blocks off' (the real Gedney House stood at Broadway and 40th Street). East or west of Fifth is our inference.
source_quote: The equality vanished, once inside the door on Thirty-Ninth Street.
source2_quote: IT was Patrick Gilligan in his hansom cab who took Lucinda around from the old Gedney House to the Misses Peters' apartment, two flights up.

household: with her parents Rose and Rafferty Dickinson
creator: Madeleine L'Engle
address_as_given: Park Avenue
notes: Fifteen-year-old Camilla narrates about three weeks in November 1950. Only 'Park Avenue' is given, with no cross street; the point is a generic residential stretch of Park Avenue on the Upper East Side. Republished in 1965 as Camilla.
source_quote: Camilla lives on Park Avenue in New York City with her wealthy parents Rose, who is beautiful yet irresponsible and overdramatic, and Rafferty, a stern, responsible architect.

household: with her parents Mona and Bill Rowan and her brother Frank
creator: Madeleine L'Engle
address_as_given: Greenwich Village
notes: Camilla's best friend Luisa lives with her bohemian, quarreling parents Mona and Bill and her older brother Frank, Camilla's love interest. No street is given.
source_quote: Luisa's family is not affluent, she lives in Greenwich Village with bohemian parents, and she is more open to discussing her family problems.

creator: Madeleine L'Engle
address_as_given: Greenwich Village
notes: Frank Rowan's friend, a young veteran who lost both legs in World War II; Frank takes Camilla to visit him. No street is given.
source_quote: He lost both of his legs in World War II and lives with his mother in Greenwich Village.

creator: Emily Cheney Neville
address_as_given: near Gramercy Park
notes: Fourteen-year-old Dave lives in an apartment with his lawyer father and asthmatic mother; his neighbor Kate keeps a houseful of stray cats. The source places the home near Gramercy Park without a street. Newbery Medal, 1964.
source_quote: Dave Mitchell is fourteen and lives with his parents in Manhattan near Gramercy Park.

creator: Mary Hays Weik
address_as_given: the top floor of a brownstone in Harlem
notes: Nine-year-old Zeke watches the Jazz Man's window across the courtyard from his family's top-floor flat. No street is given; the setting is contemporary with publication. Newbery Honor, 1967.
source_quote: The Jazz Man is the story of a nine-year-old boy named Zeke, who lives with his parents on the top floor of a brownstone in Harlem.

household: with his father and his dog Sam
creator: George Selden
address_as_given: Greenwich Village
notes: Thirteen-year-old Tim's first home, with his dog Sam and his father, before he is sent to live with his aunt on Sutton Place. No street is given.
source_quote: Timothy Farr is a 13-year-old boy living in Greenwich Village, New York , with his dog, Sam, his father, Lorenzo Jr.

creator: George Selden
address_as_given: his aunt Lucy Farr's home in Sutton Place
geocode_query: Sutton Place and East 57th Street, Manhattan
notes: Tim moves in with his Aunt Lucy, who sends his dog to the pound; the genie he frees turns the dog into a man. Sutton Place is a five-block street, so the point is its middle; no number is given.
source_quote: He goes to live with his aunt, Lucy Farr, in Sutton Place who soon gives Sam to the pound, claiming to be allergic to him.

household: with her parents and younger brother Chad
creator: Nancy Garden
address_as_given: the upscale neighborhood of Brooklyn Heights
notes: Seventeen-year-old Liza, a student at the private Foster Academy, lives with her parents and younger brother. Annie Kenyon's home is given only as 'far uptown' in Manhattan, so it is not mapped.
source_quote: Liza Winthrop : The protagonist and narrator of the novel, Liza is a 17-year-old girl living in the upscale neighborhood of Brooklyn Heights .

creator: Walter Dean Myers
address_as_given: Harlem
notes: Didi, a scholarship-bound student who wants out of Harlem, lives there with her mother; the novel's other lead, Motown, lives alone in an abandoned building in the same neighborhood. No street is given. Coretta Scott King Author Award.
source_quote: It is centered on two African-American lovers living in Harlem , New York City, as they navigate life in the ghetto life and their romantic relationship.

creator: Felice Holman
address_as_given: a room underground in the Grand Central–42nd Street subway station
geocode_query: Lexington Avenue and East 42nd Street, Manhattan
notes: Thirteen-year-old Slake runs away and lives for 121 days in a hidden room in a wall of the IRT Lexington Avenue line tunnels at Grand Central, selling newspapers he collects from trains. The input list dates the book 1986; it was first published in 1974.
source_quote: Plot Aremis Slake lives in a room underground in the subway station Grand Central – 42nd Street .

household: with his mother and sister Sassy
creator: Walter Dean Myers
address_as_given: a contemporary Harlem neighborhood
notes: Twelve-year-old Jamal lives with his mother and his sister Sassy while his brother Randy, leader of the Scorpions gang, is in jail. No street is given. Newbery Honor, 1989.
source_quote: Twelve-year-old Jamal Hicks lives in a contemporary Harlem neighborhood in which male peer tension and values can outweigh other influences, even family, church and school.

household: with her father Poppy and her grandmother Gram
creator: Patricia Reilly Giff
address_as_given: St. Albans, Queens
notes: Lily's year-round home with her father Poppy and her grandmother Gram during World War II. No street is given. Newbery Honor, 1998.
source_quote: Lily lives in St. Albans, Queens with her father and grandmother.
source2_quote: Lily lives in St. Albans, Queens, with her father and her grandmother.

household: with her grandmother Gram (and her father, until he ships out)
creator: Patricia Reilly Giff
address_as_given: Gram's summer house in Rockaway, by the Atlantic Ocean
notes: The family's summer house, where Lily meets the Hungarian refugee Albert in the summer of 1944. BookRags describes it as a house on stilts near the ocean. The publisher says only Rockaway; Wikipedia says Far Rockaway, so the point sits there with a wide radius.
source_quote: Each summer Lily and her father (Poppy) stay in Far Rockaway near the Atlantic Ocean at her grandmother's (Gram) house.
source2_quote: As in past years, Lily will spend the summer in Rockaway, in her family’s summer house by the Atlantic Ocean.

creator: Gail Carson Levine
address_as_given: the Hebrew Home for Boys, on the edge of Harlem
notes: After his father's death in October 1926, eleven-year-old Dave is placed in the fictional Hebrew Home for Boys and sneaks out at night into the Harlem Renaissance. Wikipedia says the real orphanage behind it, where Levine's father grew up, was the Hebrew Orphan Asylum, which stood on Amsterdam Avenue at 136th-138th Streets (now demolished); the point sits there as an inference, not a location named in the novel.
source_quote: Knowing only that her father grew up in an orphanage in New York on the edge of Harlem, Levine (Ella Enchanted, 1997) weaves a tale
source2_quote: The Hebrew Orphan Asylum was the name of the actual orphanage that Levine's father grew up in, not the Hebrew Home for Boys.

creator: Nick McDonell
address_as_given: Manhattan's Upper East Side
notes: Seventeen-year-old White Mike, a restaurateur's son who deals marijuana to rich private-school kids, lives with his father; the novel covers the days between Christmas and New Year's Eve 1999. No street is given.
source_quote: "White Mike" dresses in an overcoat and lives with his dad on Manhattan's Upper East Side (his mom died of breast cancer not too long ago).

work: The Earth, My Butt, and Other Big Round Things
creator: Carolyn Mackler
address_as_given: a penthouse apartment on Riverside Drive
notes: Fifteen-year-old Ginny lives with her parents in a penthouse; her private school, Brewster, is on the Upper East Side. The source gives Riverside Drive but no cross street, so the point is a midpoint of the Upper West Side stretch of the Drive.
source_quote: Virginia lives on the Upper West Side, in a penthouse apartment on Riverside Drive (read: her family is rich), and Brewster, her elite private school, is on the Upper East Side.

household: with Maddy Carter and Sal Vikram
creator: Alex Scarrow
address_as_given: their field office underneath an archway of the Williamsburg Bridge
notes: Liam, Maddy Carter and Sal Vikram live and work in the agency's base in a railway arch under the bridge, looping through September 10-11, 2001; the same base is home in the sequels, including The Doomsday Code (2011). Wikipedia elsewhere calls it the 'Brooklyn archway', so the point sits under the Brooklyn approach of the bridge.
source_quote: They operate from their field office underneath an archway of the Williamsburg Bridge in New York City in a two-day 'Time Bubble' , on September 10 and 11, 2001 .
source2_quote: placing a bear from a shop window near the Brooklyn archway in her recruitment memory.

household: with her daughter and her father
creator: N. K. Jemisin
address_as_given: Bedford Stuyvesant, where Brooklyn owns two brownstones
notes: The avatar of Brooklyn, a former rapper turned lawyer and city councilwoman, lives here with her daughter and her ailing father. No street is given; the setting is contemporary with publication.
source_quote: Manny, Brooklyn, and Padmini take a Lyft to Bedford Stuyvesant, where Brooklyn owns two brownstones.

creator: N. K. Jemisin
address_as_given: a four-story walk-up in Jackson Heights, in her aunt Aishwarya's place
notes: The avatar of Queens, a Tamil graduate student, lives in her aunt's apartment between the third and fourth floors of a walk-up the novel treats as a microcosm of Queens. The quote is from the novel as excerpted in the review. The novel's Staten Island avatar, Aislyn Houlihan, lives with her parents on Staten Island, but no neighborhood is given, so she is not mapped.
source_quote: This is just one building amid thousands in Jackson Heights — but here, in this four-story walk-up, is a microcosm of Queens itself.
source2_quote: And somewhere between the third floor and the fourth, where Padmini lives in Aishwarya’s place, Manny gets it.

creator: Jacqueline Woodson
address_as_given: Harlem
notes: Three orphaned brothers live together in Harlem, with the oldest, Ty'ree, as guardian. No street is given; the point is central Harlem. Setting years are estimated from the publication date.
source_quote: growing up without parents in Harlem
